question: Law 36/2011, regulating social jurisdiction, establishes a series of guarantees for legal costs aimed at ensuring more equitable access to justice for workers, especially those with limited resources, in accordance with EU law However, there are no equivalent guarantees for public-sector workers, including temporary staff, who are forced to process their cases through administrative justice, which leads to issues with impartiality as they are judged by officials from outside the area of labour law, and are penalised in terms of the costs, which are particularly high.
Could this situation be interpreted as discrimination in violation of the principle of equality of treatment, a fundamental principle of the EU?
Does the lack of equal guarantees for public-sector workers and temporary staff in comparison with other workers constitute unjustified discrimination on the basis of their employment conditions?

Given that government workers are the main complainants and whistle-blowers in such instances of non-compliance, could this discrimination be understood to be an implicit reprisal against government employees who denounce breaches of EU law, and ECJ rulings in particular?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.7.2024) Under Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU (the Charter1), everyone whose rights guaranteed by EU law are violated has the right to an effective remedy, including the right to legal aid for those who lack sufficient resources.

In line with Article 51(1) thereof, an individual may rely on Article 47 in the context of proceedings before national courts if these are related to the alleged violation, application or implementation of EU law.

The Commission notes that there is no specific secondary EU legislation regulating legal aid in administrative cases, and that the EU acquis on fixed-term work2 does not apply in the case raised by the Honourable Member because the concept of employment conditions as interpreted by the Court of Justice of the EU does not cover the conditions for access to justice.

Article 20(1)(c) of Directive 2019/19373 requires Member States to ensure that whistleblowers have access, as appropriate, to legal aid in criminal and in cross-border civil proceedings in accordance with Directive (EU) 2016/1919 and Directive 2008/52/EC, and to legal aid in further proceedings, in accordance with national law.

This Article has to be interpreted in light of Article 47 of the Charter which leaves to the Member States, within the framework of the organisation of their national justice system, a free choice of the means to be used in guaranteeing legal aid, including the payment of court fees, in so far as such aid is necessary to ensure effective access to justice.
1 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf 2 Clause 4 of the Framework Agreement annexed to Council Directive 1999/70/EC on fixed-term work, which

prohibits less favourable treatment of fixed-term (i.e. temporary) workers than comparable permanent workers in respect of their employment conditions solely because they have a fixed-term contract unless different treatment is justified on objective grounds. Moreover, the Commission notes that the rules on legal costs described by the Honourable Member seem to apply generally to fixed-term and to permanent workers.

Situations such as this, which are not linked to the fixed-term nature of employment are not covered by the Framework Agreement. 3 Directive (EU) 2019/1937 of 23 October 2019 on the protection of persons who report breaches of Union law, OJ L 305.
